title: K1 P1 ribbing
subtitle: The most elastic of the basic ribbing structures.
excerpt: K1 P1 ribbing alternates one knit stitch and one purl stitch across every row. It is the standard brim for hats and cuffs, valued for its elasticity and its neat, fine-column appearance.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Knitter, Series 1 (1886). Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938). Beeton's Book of Needlework (1870).

glossaryTerms.definition: A stitch pattern worked by alternating one knit stitch and one purl stitch across every row. The knit stitches form raised vertical columns and the purl stitches recede, producing a stretchy, ridged fabric.

content.text: K1 P1 ribbing (abbreviated k1, p1 rib) alternates one knit stitch and one purl stitch across every row. The

fabric is reversible in appearance (the columns simply shift one stitch when turned) and distinctly elastic because the knit and purl columns pull against each other in the horizontal direction. The main skill beyond the two individual stitches is remembering to move the yarn between the needles as you switch from knit to purl and back. Difficulty: beginner.
An even number of cast-on stitches
Cast on an even number of stitches.
Row 1: (k1, p1) across. Before each purl stitch, bring the yarn forward between the needles. Before each knit stitch, take the yarn back.
Row 2: knit the knit stitches and purl the purl stitches as they appear. The raised V column gets a knit; the recessed bump gets a purl.
Repeat Row 2 for the length of ribbing needed.

K1 P1 ribbing is the standard brim on fine-gauge hats and the preferred cuff for fitted sweater sleeves. It appears on the welt (lower edge) of jerseys where a narrow, tight entry is needed. In sock patterns it typically works the leg and cuff above the heel. The 2x2 variant gives a more pronounced column and slightly less cling; which to choose depends on the pattern's intended fit.

items.symptom: Extra stitches appear because the yarn was not moved between stitches
items.cause: Forgetting to move the yarn between needles when switching from knit to purl
items.fix: Before each purl stitch, confirm the yarn is at the front; before each knit stitch, confirm it is at the back. Saying the position aloud helps when learning.

items.symptom: Columns wobble: a knit column has a purl bump in it
items.cause: Purling a knit stitch or knitting a purl stitch on row 2
items.fix: Read the stitches on the needle rather than counting rows. The raised V column = knit; the horizontal bump = purl.

items.cause: Working too tightly, or using a yarn without elasticity (cotton, linen)
items.fix: Try working on a needle one size larger. Woollen or wool-blend yarn will always rib more elastically than plant fibres.
